title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
prompt: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. As a follow-up: given an already-sorted, non-overlapping set of intervals, insert a new interval and merge as needed.
blurb: Sort by start, then sweep once and coalesce — the canonical interval-merging pattern with an insert-interval twist.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Clarifies whether touching endpoints ([1,4],[4,5]) count as overlapping, and whether the input is pre-sorted.

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Sort by start time, then linear sweep merging when current.start <= last.end. Recognizes sorting is the enabling insight.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Merges by taking max of ends (handles fully-nested intervals), extends the open interval in place, and starts a new one only when there's a real gap.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: O(n log n) dominated by the sort; O(n) or O(sort) space. For the sorted follow-up, notes O(n) single pass with no sort.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean sweep with a single 'last merged' reference; no repeated index juggling; readable comparison.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Empty input, single interval, fully-nested interval, touching endpoints, all-overlapping, all-disjoint.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Tests nested and touching cases explicitly, not just the happy path.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Explains why max(end) matters and walks a small example through the sweep.

constraints: Intervals may be given in any order and may be nested or touching

examples.explanation: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap (2 <= 3) and merge into [1,6]. The rest are disjoint.
They touch at 4; treated as overlapping and merged.

test_cases.expected: [[1,4]] — [2,3] is fully nested inside [1,4]; end must stay 4, not 3

reference.optimal_time: O(n log n) for merge (sort-bound); O(n) for insert into a pre-sorted list
reference.optimal_space: O(n) for the output (or O(log n)-O(n) auxiliary for the sort)

approaches.name: brute force (pairwise merge to fixpoint)
approaches.idea: Repeatedly scan all pairs, merge any overlapping pair, and restart until no merges happen in a full pass.

approaches.name: optimal: sort + linear sweep
approaches.idea: Sort intervals by start. Initialize result with the first interval. For each next interval, if its start <= result.last.end, extend result.last.end = max(result.last.end, interval.end); otherwise append it as a new interval. Sorting guarantees any overlap is with the most recently appended interval, so one pass suffices.

approaches.name: insert-interval (sorted input, no sort)
approaches.idea: Single pass over the sorted, non-overlapping list in three phases: (1) append all intervals ending before newInterval.start; (2) merge all intervals overlapping newInterval by expanding newInterval.start=min(...), newInterval.end=max(...), then append it once; (3) append all remaining intervals starting after newInterval.end.

follow_ups: Insert Interval into an already-sorted, non-overlapping list in O(n) without re-sorting (the three-phase sweep above).
Given many intervals, find the minimum number of conference rooms needed (min-heap of end times, or the sweep-line +1/-1 events).
Interval intersection: given two sorted interval lists, return their pairwise intersections (two-pointer).
Employee free time: merge across all employees' busy intervals, then return the gaps.
Streaming variant: maintain merged intervals as new ones arrive online (balanced BST / interval tree keyed by start).
reference.reference_solution: merge(intervals): sort intervals by start ascending. result = [intervals[0]]. for each iv in intervals[1:]: last = result[-1]; if iv.start <= last.end: last.end = max(last.end, iv.end)  // in-place extend; handles nested intervals via max; else: result.append(iv). return result. The max on end is the subtle correctness point: a nested interval [2,3] inside [1,4] must not shrink the end to 3. Touching endpoints merge because the comparison uses <=; if the problem says touching should NOT merge, use strict <. Follow-up insert(intervals, newIv): res=[]; i=0; n=len(intervals); while i<n and intervals[i].end < newIv.start: res.append(intervals[i]); i++. while i<n and intervals[i].start <= newIv.end: newIv.start=min(newIv.start,intervals[i].start); newIv.end=max(newIv.end,intervals[i].end); i++. res.append(newIv). while i<n: res.append(intervals[i]); i++. return res.
pitfalls: Using interval.end instead of max(last.end, interval.end) — breaks on nested intervals.
Sorting by end instead of start, which breaks the 'overlap is only with the last appended' invariant.
Off-by-one on the touching case: decide < vs <= deliberately based on the clarified definition.
Mutating the input while iterating in the brute-force version.

interviewer_notes: First signal: do they ask whether touching intervals merge and whether input is sorted? If they don't, let them assume, then challenge with [[1,4],[4,5]] during testing. Stay silent through the sort-and-sweep; the one nudge worth giving if they use interval.end instead of max is to hand them the nested test [[1,4],[2,3]] and ask what it returns. Once merge is clean and correct, escalate to the Insert Interval follow-up and push for the O(n) no-re-sort three-phase solution — that separates mid from senior. If they finish that fast, go to meeting-rooms-II (min-heap) as a heap-warm-up.
